title: The Depth Poset Under Transpositions in the Filter
abstract: The depth poset of a filtered Lefschetz complex reflects the dependencies between the cancellations of different shallow birth-death pairs. Using the fast algorithms for computing the depth poset in [Edelsbrunner et al., 2026] and for updating the persistence diagram under transpositions in [Cohen-Steiner et al., 2006], we give a complete case analysis of how transpositions of cells in the filter affect the depth poset. In addition, we present statistics on the depth poset for random point data and its sensitivity to the transpositions that occur in random straight-line homotopies.

      Abstract
The depth poset of a filtered Lefschetz complex reflects the dependencies between the cancellations
of different shallow birth-death pairs. Using the fast algorithms for computing the depth poset
in [9] and for updating the persistence diagram under transpositions in [7], we give a complete case
analysis of how transpositions of cells in the filter affect the depth poset. In addition, we present
statistics on the depth poset for random point data and its sensitivity to the transpositions that
occur in random straight-line homotopies.

 1      Introduction
The field of topology optimization aims at the design of shapes whose large- and small-scale
connectivity is subject to modifications applied in order to satisfy constraints and optimize
objective functions. The traditional approach is numerical and optimizes through repeated
local improvement; see the text by Bendsøe [4] and the major revision by Bendsøe and
Sigmund [5]. More recently, the methods of topological data analysis have matured and
provide an alternative approach to this seasoned problem; see e.g. the “big steps” algorithm
by Nigmetov and Morozov [19], which is closely related to the work presented in this paper.
Specifically, we aim at exploring the space of shapes that relate to each other through the

       cancellation and interchange of the critical points of a function. This is naturally related to
       the simplification of functions and shapes, as studied in [1, 3, 11], but goes beyond this work
       by casting light on the space of possible simplifications.
          An overarching goal for the presented work is to uncover the potential new tools from
       combinatorial dynamics pioneered by Forman [13, 12], offering discrete counterparts for classic
       concepts such as the Conley index, Morse decomposition, and connection matrix [16, 17, 18].
          The primary technical prerequisites for our work are the depth poset of a filter on a
       complex, as introduced in [9], the well established concept of persistent homology; see the text
       by Edelsbrunner and Harer [10], and the vineyard algorithm for computing persistence along
       a parametrized family of functions, as originally described in [7]. The depth poset collects all
       dependencies between cancellations of shallow birth-death pairs (formerly known as apparent
       pairs [2] and close pairs [8]) and thus provides a global yet discrete representation of the
       space of shapes reachable by sequences of such cancellations. We mention that shallow pairs
       appeared in other seemingly unrelated contexts, for example in fast adaptive sorting [20].
       Our main contribution is the complete case analysis of how transpositions in the filter affect
       the depth poset. Working toward establishing the depth poset as a first class object, we also
       present statistics on the size and shape of this poset and its variation under transpositions.

       Outline. Section 2 explains the technical background needed for our results. Section 3 gives
       the complete case analysis of how a transposition in the filter affects the depth poset of
       the same. Section 4 presents statistical results that probe the depth poset and homotopies
       between them for random PL height functions on Delaunay mosaics of Poisson point processes.


        2     Background
       This section presents the background we need to study the relations and orders in which our
       results are couched. Besides standard material, we need concepts from persistent homology
       and its matrix reduction algorithms. We refer to [10] for more comprehensive background.

       Relations. We adapt the terminology from graph theory, in which a relation consists of
       (directed) arcs that connect nodes. Each arc goes from its source to its target, both of which
       are nodes. A (directed) path is a sequence of arcs such that the target of each arc is the
       source of the next arc, and it goes from the source of the first arc to the target of the last
       arc. It is a directed cycle if the target of the last arc is also the source of the first arc. The
       relation is acyclic if it has no directed cycle. Note however that an acyclic relation may have
       undirected cycles, such as two disjoint paths that connect the same two nodes.
           An acyclic relation has a unique transitive closure, which is the possibly larger (acyclic)
       relation that has an arc from a source to a target whenever there is such a path. A partial
       order is an acyclic relation that is its own transitive closure, and in situations where we wish
       to emphasize the nodes rather than the arcs, we refer to it as a partially ordered set, or a
       poset, for short. Two nodes in a poset are comparable if there is an arc that connects them,
       and we write a ≤ b if a is the source and b is the target of the connecting arc. A total order
       is a partial order in which any two nodes are comparable. It is a linear extension of a partial
       order on the same nodes if a ≤ b in the partial order implies a ≤ b in the total order.
           In this paper we work with Lefschetz complexes with coefficients in Z/2Z for simplicity,
       which can be viewed as chain complexes with a fixed bases. In particular, they avoid the
       complications that come with concrete geometric descriptions of the cells. This type of
       complex was introduced first under the more modest name of a complex in the book by
       Lefschetz [15]. We borrow the below definition from [9].

Persistent Homology and Transpositions. Given a filter on a complex, f : K → R, we
construct the complex by adding one cell at a time following the implied order. After
adding i cells, we arrive at a subcomplex Ki ⊆ K, and we refer to the resulting sequence of
subcomplexes as a filtration of K. Fixing a dimension, p, and a coefficient field, e.g. Z/2Z,
we apply the degree-p homology functor to each subcomplex and thus get a linear sequence
of vector spaces connected by linear maps:

    Hp (∅) = Hp (K0 ) → Hp (K1 ) → . . . → Hp (Kn ) = Hp (K);                                              (1)

see e.g. [14] for the needed background in algebraic topology. Whenever the added cell
has dimension p, it either gives birth to a degree-p homology class or it gives death to a
degree-(p − 1) homology class. This is classic Morse theory, and the novelty in persistence
is that for each death-giving (p + 1)-cell we find a unique birth-giving p-cell whose class it
ends. We call these the degree-p birth-death pairs of f , denoted BD p (f ). It is also possible
that some birth-giving p-cells do not get paired, and they reflect the degree-p homology of
K. A convenient combinatorial representation of this information is the persistence diagram,
denoted Dgmp (f ), which maps (a, b) ∈ BD p (f ) to the point (f (a), f (b)) ∈ R2 .
    An important property is the stability of the persistence diagram, originally proved
in [6]. In a nutshell, it says that for two monotonic functions, f, g : K → R, there is a
bijection between Dgmp (f ) and Dgmp (g) such that the maximum coordinate difference
between corresponding points is bounded from above by the absolute maximum of f (a) − g(a)
over all cells a ∈ K. This will be instrumental in the following construction.

           Consider two filters, f0 , f1 : K → R, and the straight-line homotopy defined by fλ (a) =
       (1 − λ)f0 (a) + λf1 (a) for 0 ≤ λ ≤ 1. These functions imply a 1-parameter family of
       persistence diagrams for each dimension p. Mapping every point (fλ (a), fλ (b)) ∈ Dgmp (fλ )
       to (fλ (a), fλ (b), λ) ∈ R3 , we effectively stack up these diagrams, and because of stability, the
       points form continuous curves in R3 . Following the terminology in [7], we call these curves
       vines and the collection of vines a vineyard. Assuming K is finite, there are only finitely
       many values of λ for which fλ is not a filter (because it assigns the same value to at least
       two cells). These values split [0, 1] into finitely many open intervals with a unique ordering
       of the cells in each. In the generic case, the orderings in any two consecutive intervals differ
       by a single transposition of two adjacent cells. Such a transposition may or may not affect
       the birth-death pairs, and if it does, we call it a switch. As established in [7], there are only
       three kinds of switches: the BB-type, which swaps the birth-giving cells between two pairs,
       the DD-type, which swaps the death-giving cells between two pairs, and the BD-type, which
       swaps a birth-giving with a death-giving cell; see Figure 2. Observe that in the first two
       cases, the two affected points belong to the same-degree persistence diagram, while in the
       third case the affected points belong to persistence diagrams of consecutive degrees.

       Cancellation of Shallow Pairs. Given a filtered Lefschetz complex, we are interested
       in simplifying it. The natural operation to this end is the cancellation of a cell b with
       one of its facets a. The operation produces a new Lefschetz complex (K ′ , dim′ , κ′ ) where
       K ′ = K \ {a, b}, dim′ is the restriction of dim to K ′ , and the new incidence map is defined
       for x, y ∈ K ′ by κ′ (y, x) = κ(y, x) + κ(y, a) · κ(b, x); see the schematic cancellation of the
       pair (a, b) in Figure 3.

          A cancellation may have side-effects, such as changing the homotopy type of the complex
       or making a cell a facet of another cell that precedes it in the filter. In contrast, a cancellation
       preserves the homology of the Lefschetz complex [9]. To avoid the need to reorganize the
H. Edelsbrunner, M. Lipiński, M. Mrozek, M. Soriano-Trigueros, and F. Zimin                             41:5


filter, we restrict ourselves to cancellations where this is not necessary. Even more, we restrict
ourselves to canceling shallow pairs, a ≺ b, for which a is the last facet of b and b is the first
cofacet of a in the ordering of the filter; see [9] but also [2], where they are referred to as
apparent pairs. If a ≺ b is a shallow pair, then all other facets of b precede a and all other
cofacets of a succeed b, so the new filter is obtained by removing a and b, and no reordering
is necessary. The following basic properties are obvious or proved in [9]:
     every shallow pair is a birth-death pair of the filter;
     after a shallow pair is canceled, the remaining birth-death pairs are unchanged;
     there is at least one shallow pair, unless the face relation is empty.
Because of the third property, we can keep canceling shallow pairs until the face relation
runs empty. We call the resulting sequence of canceled pairs a shallow cancellation order,
which by the first two properties is a total order of the birth-death pairs of the original filter.
However, there may be many orderings of the birth-death pairs such that each pair is shallow
at the time it gets canceled, which motivates the next concept.
▶ Definition 2.2. The depth poset of a filter on a Lefschetz complex, f : K → R, is the
intersection of all shallow cancellation orders of f , denoted Depth(f ).
This concept was introduced in [9], along with some of its fundamental properties, which we
state without proof.
▶ Lemma 2.3. Let f : K → R be a filter on a Lefschetz complex, φ = (x, y) and ψ = (a, b)
two birth-death pairs of f , (φ, ψ) an arc in Depth(f ), σ = (s, t) a shallow pair of f , and
f ′ : K \ {s, t} the filter after canceling σ. Then
 1. nodes connected by an arc in Depth(f ) are nested; that is: f (a) < f (x) < f (y) < f (b);
 2. arcs of Depth(f ) respect dimensions; that is: dim a = dim x and dim b = dim y;
 3. canceling σ has no side-effects; that is: Depth(f ′ ) = Depth(f ) ∩ [BD(f ′ ) × BD(f ′ )].
By Property 2, Depth(f ) is the disjoint union of posets Depthp (f ) ⊆ BD p (f ) × BD p (f ).

Matrix Reduction Twice. While the definition of the depth poset is constructive, it is in
terms of possibly exponentially many total orders on the birth-death pairs. Alternatively, it
can be constructed as the transitive closure of two relations, both of which can be computed
efficiently by reducing the boundary matrix of the complex. We review the algorithms and
refer to [9] for a proof of correctness.
▶ Definition 2.4. The death relation of a filter on a Lefschetz complex, f : K → R, denoted
D(f ) ⊆ BD(f ) × BD(f ), records the left-to-right column operations during the reduction of
the boundary matrix in reverse order of the birth-giving cells; see Algorithm 1.
The arcs in the death relation correspond to the off-diagonal non-zero entries in the columns
of death-giving cells in U1 :

   D(f ) = {((x, y), (a, b)) ∈ BD(f ) × BD(f ) | y ̸= b and U1 [y, b] = 1}.                    (2)

To make sense of U1 , consider the matrix V1 that stores the chains whose boundaries are
the cycles in R1 . Initially, V1 is the identity matrix and we maintain it by applying the
same column operations as performed on R1 . If we ignore the deletions of rows and columns,
we retain the matrices in their original sizes, and it is not difficult to see that they satisfy
R1 = ∆V1 and ∆ = R1 U1 throughout the algorithm, so U1 = V1−1 .
▶ Definition 2.5. The birth relation of a filter on a Lefschetz complex, f : K → R, denoted
B(f ) ⊆ BD(f ) × BD(f ), records the bottom-to-top row operations during the reduction of
the boundary matrix in the order of the death-giving cells; see Algorithm 2.

             Algorithm 1 Bottom to Top Column Reduction.
             Input: ∆ (the boundary matrix)
             Output: R1 U1 (a decomposition of ∆)
        1: R1 = ∆; U1 = Id;

       depth poset as the transitive closure of their union; see [9] for a proof. This is important so

a complete case analysis along the classification of transpositions into three types: of two
birth-giving cells, of two death-giving cells, and of a birth-giving with a death-giving cell.
    Prior to the case analysis, we state two lemmas that will both be repeatedly used. The
first excludes certain configurations of birth-death pairs.

▶ Lemma 3.1. Let f : K → R be a filter on a Lefschetz complex, and a ≺ y two cells in
K. If a is the last facet of y in the ordering implied by f , and a is not yet paired when we
encounter y in the ordering of the filter, then (a, y) is a birth-death pair of f .

Proof. Consider the standard matrix reduction algorithm for persistent homology, which
reduces the columns of the ordered boundary matrix from left to right. Since a is the last
facet of y, the lowest non-zero entry in column y is in row a. When the algorithm arrives at
y, a is not yet paired, so there is no pivot in its row. It follows that this entry remains and
becomes a pivot, which is equivalent to (a, y) becoming a birth-death pair.                   ◀

    The second lemma addresses a property of ordered boundary matrices that amounts to a
reformulation of Lemma 4.6 in [9]. We state it without proof.

▶ Lemma 3.2. Let f : K → R be a filter on a Lefschetz complex, ∆ the corresponding ordered
boundary matrix, x a row of ∆, and y a column of ∆. Then any two boundary matrices
obtained by canceling all birth-death pairs with pivots below row x or to the left of column y
following shallow but possibly different cancellation orders are the same.

 5     Discussion
The main contribution of this paper is the complete analysis of how transpositions of cells
in the filter affect the depth poset of a filtered Lefschetz complex. This analysis provides
further evidence for the relative significance of birth-death switches, as they mark a more
extensive re-organization of the persistent homology than all other types of transpositions.
Our initial computational experiments suggest that the birth-death switches are more rare
than all other types, and that the number of arcs that change grows much slower than the
total number of arcs in the depth poset. This work calls for further research in at least the
following three directions:
    investigate the links between the transposition induced changes in the depth poset and
    the bifurcations in the associated gradient dynamics;
    extend the notion of a depth poset from discrete Morse functions to discrete vector fields
    as introduced in Forman [12], or even to multi-vector fields as studied in [16, 17];
    study the depth poset stochastically for various models of random functions and for
    homotopies between them.
We finally mention that the algorithms in this paper and its precursor [9] are closely related
to the algorithms for topology optimization described by Nigmetov and Morozov [19]. Can
the more global topological information provided by the depth poset be harvested to get
faster or better methods for topology optimization?
